### The checker

The checker is built in: the `tsrs` crates (`tsrs_api`, `tsrs_vfs`, pinned `=0.24.0`, TypeScript `3e9236361fa9`, the commit of `typescript@7.1.0-beta`) linked into the CLI and the napi binding. Nothing is installed and no project `typescript` is looked for. It runs by default since S8.

- **Its own threads.** `crates/semantic/src/checker.rs` creates a `tsrs_api::Session` on a thread of its own with a 512 MiB stack, the stack the `tsrs` binary serves on: a query runs on the calling thread, and a type 2,000 deep overflows a default 2 MiB thread, which aborts the process. Requests from any thread reach it over a channel and are answered one at a time; a whole-project `extract` starts a second thread with a channel (a lane) of its own and asks two programs over the same root files, each program's requests down its own lane (`tsrs_api` locks a program's one checker for the length of a request, so two programs are what can be answered at once). Each program has a snapshot of its own (`Rpc::open_programs`): `tsrs_api` registers the handles it hands out in one table per snapshot, behind one lock, which two programs of one snapshot waited on. The second snapshot is derived from the first (`updateSnapshot` with `createPrograms`), so it reads every file from the first's cache, as the first read it, and neither goes to the disk again nor parses a file again: a second `createSnapshot` repeated the file system work of a program build (stat, lstat and read of every file it resolves), which took 25 to 35 ms and raised the run's system CPU time. Every program holds every root file, so either answers a component as one program would; the Storybook session asks one; `Session::handle_request` is the dispatcher the `tsrs` binary serves, so `rpc.rs` sends the methods and JSON of `tsc --api`. A stack overflow aborts and cannot be caught (deep-type tests: 2,000 levels in every run, 10,000 in release).
- **Guards** (trail 369 slice 2). A panic inside the checker comes back as an error for that request (`tsrs_api` catches it, and the thread catches any that escapes), then every lane of the session stops (a whole-project run fails on the first lane's error and answers structurally, with one diagnostic) and the last to leave closes the session: a session a panic unwound through is not asked again, and in a Storybook session the next request starts a fresh one (three crashes and the checker stays down for the session). A panic `tsrs` reports as the client's fault (an unknown `moduleResolution`) is an error like any other and the session is kept. `tsrs` parses on threads of its own with 256 MiB stacks, which a file nested a few hundred thousand levels deep overflows (measured: an object type 200,000 deep parses, 300,000 aborts; generic, tuple, JSX and arrow chains abort between 300,000 and 1,000,000); so every file the checker reads from the disk is measured first, its deepest nesting of `(`, `[` and `{` and, apart, of `<` (5 ms for Chakra's 4.7 MB of declarations, whose deepest is 187), and a request that read one past 20,000 fails with a `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning naming it, its components keeping their structural answer. Requests that build snapshots, the ones that read files, run one at a time across the lanes, so a refusal is attributed to the request that met it. A snapshot the refused request made is released before the error goes back, as is one made for a caller that stopped waiting: its id never reaches anyone who could release it. Nesting written without brackets (a chain of arrow types, `a ? b : …`, `1 + 1 + …`) is not measured.
- **Lib files.** The crates embed TypeScript's lib, so a lib declaration's file is `bundled:///libs/lib.dom.d.ts`. The path classifiers read the file name (`lib.*.d.ts`), so it is the lib (`tests/tsrs_real.rs`).
- **Failures.** A checker thread that cannot start, a request past its deadline and a stopped checker give one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning.
- **One checker.** The product has no other route: `--tsc-path` (`tscPath`), which ran a `tsc --api` binary as a process through `crates/tsc-client`, and the version allow-list it was checked against were removed in trail 369 slice 4 (the "Spawn the tsrs binary" alternative of ADR 0026 stays rejected). The Go `typescript@7.1.0-beta` runs only in `apps/oracle`, as the oracle, the construct goldens and `construct:parity`, which compares it with the npm `tsrs` of the same release as the pinned crates (`scripts/check-packaging.mjs` holds the two pins equal).
- **A kept answer for `extract`.** The linked checker reads the disk only through the file system `checker.rs` hands its session, so a whole-project `extract` with the cache on hands it one that notes every question it asks and a digest of each answer (`crates/semantic/src/kept.rs`): a file's text, whether a path is a file or a directory, a directory's entries, a path's metadata and real path. Failed lookups are questions too (the paths module resolution tried and did not find), and so are the tsconfig and what it extends. The answer is kept beside the parse cache (`checker-answers.msgpack` in the cache directory, `SemanticOutcome::to_bytes`) with those questions, under this build's fingerprint (`crates/semantic/build.rs`: its sources and `Cargo.lock`, so the pinned `tsrs` too) and a key of the request (the components with what the structural pass says of them, the project root, the tsconfig's path). The next run asks every question again of the disk, in parallel, and uses the kept answer only when each is answered the same: any change where the checker looked, a new file where it found none included, discards it whole. It is the whole program's or nothing, never per component, since a component's dependency closure is not known (ADR 0026); this is the dependency set Go's `trackingvfs` records for watch mode, kept with digests of what was read. A run whose checker read one path two ways (a file edited while it ran) or that reports a diagnostic keeps nothing; `--no-cache` neither reads nor writes it; `check`, `inspect` and the Storybook session never use it. Both programs of the run read through it: the second program's snapshot is derived from the first's and reads its files from that cache, so the questions the first asked cover both, and a file the session is refused for its nesting (the guard above) spoils the notes, so nothing is kept for that run. The answer is written before a one-shot run forgets its programs (`Teardown::OneShot`). A rerun over unchanged files costs the structural pass, the check of the questions (about 50 ms on `gate-large`) and the merge: 0.25 s against 1.44 s cold (`docs/gate-measurements.md`).

The client sends `createPrograms[].compilerOptions` (the Node client sends `options`; the server accepts both, and `crates/semantic/tests/resolve.rs` pins the key). Every test that asks a checker (`resolve`, `tsrs_real`, `cases`, `families`, `declared`, `memo`, `exports`, `composes`, `instantiate`, `watch`, `on_demand`) asks the built-in one.

## On demand, per component (on by default)

A long-lived session (the Storybook addon, the lazy `WatchSession`) attaches a warm checker instead of running the whole-project pass above (ADR 0022): a napi session does unless `checker: false`. `caliper-docgen-semantic` keeps one checker warm behind a worker thread, answers from a program rooted at only the requested component's file, and returns its props. The program's snapshot is kept between requests and brought up to date with the files the session says changed ("Watch", below). `WatchSession::component` merges them into the structural answer by name (the checker's type wins, a structural prop the checker did not return stays, and `htmlAttributes` applies once after the merge, as in the structural pass) when they arrive within `semanticWaitMs` (default 150 ms), or within `semanticWaitEmptyMs` (default 2,000 ms, never less than `semanticWaitMs`) when the structural answer lists no props at all (a `ComponentProps<typeof Button>` of a package the structural pass does not model, whose props type it could not expand); otherwise it returns the structural answer plus an `Info` diagnostic, and the checker's late answer serves the next request of the same component while no source file has changed. A kept answer carries what the checker said about the request that made it (a warning that it was not told about an edit, why a component kept its structural result), and every request it serves reports that again, a late answer's included; only an unavailable checker's warning is said once per session. There is one request in flight per component key and content hash of its file: a caller that asks while it is in flight (a story asked while its own prefetch runs, or two stories of one component) waits for that answer, so the checker answers it once. The checker answers interactive requests (`WatchSession::component`, `components`) before background ones (`components_in_background`, which `sessionPrefetch` and the addon's background prefetch of the next stories use, and which waits for nobody), first come first served within each; an interactive caller that joins a background request raises it, and after 4 interactive answers in a row while background requests wait, the oldest of them goes next. Any source-file change, including a file the component only imports, drops every checker answer, so the next request asks again; an answer still in flight at that moment is neither kept nor joined. The component's structural diagnostics that the checker's props supersede are dropped when they replace the structural ones, except while a structural prop the checker did not return is still opaque: those diagnostics name the component, not the prop, so they stay until nothing they could be about is left. (The whole-project merge drops unreturned structural props, so it has no such case.) Which ones are superseded is in "Diagnostics a checker answer supersedes".

Measured with `crates/semantic/examples/ondemand_bench.rs` (50 random components, TypeScript 7.1.0-beta): the first answer takes 82 to 137 ms (Chakra 703 ms), a component asked for alone 21 to 41 ms (Chakra 534 ms), and 2 to 9 ms when asked for in batches of 8 to 32. Where the structural pass is behind (shadcn) the checker reports 2.3 times the props; where it is not (Mantine, Chakra, Spectrum) it reports the same count. The in-memory cache, the 64-program replacement and the failure modes are in the ADR. (These numbers were measured over the `tsc --api` pipe, before the checker was linked in.)

Hardening of the on-demand checker:

- **Versions:** the checker is the pinned `tsrs` crates; nothing is read from the project.
- **Memory** (trail 369 slice 2): after the first request and every fourth, once the reply is sent, the worker reads what the checker holds and compares it with `OnDemandConfig::max_rss_mib` (768 MiB). The bound is between requests: one request that needs more finishes first. This process's resident memory is the host's as well (Node, Storybook, and Caliper's own answers, which grow by about 5.5 MiB per Chakra component asked), so what is read is the resident part of the one address range `tsrs` carves its arenas from (`mincore`, about 6 ms). Past the bound the checker stops for the session: every later request keeps the structural answer, with a `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning that names the bound. It is never replaced, because a fresh session does not lower what this process holds: a closed session gives back part of its arenas (Chakra's 46 MiB fell to 22 to 37), and the fresh one parses every file again. Measured on Chakra (`docs/gate-measurements.md`): 650 edits peak at 377 MiB never replaced against 514 MiB replaced every 64 programs, and the arenas stay at 46 MiB over 2,000 edits and reach 165 MiB over 937 Chakra and MUI components. The range is the process's, so it covers every program and lane of the session; the bound is applied by the Storybook session's warm checker (one lane), and stopping it stops all of it. A whole-project `extract` (two lanes) has no arena bound, since it ends with its process; it has a heap budget instead.
- **Heap budget** (trail 404): a whole-project run (`resolve`, `resolve_cached`, `resolve_early`, which `extract` and `check` call) reads what mimalloc has committed (`mi_process_info`, about 0.9 µs) before each component and every 32 steps, a step being a checker request or a type the converter converts or recalls from its memo. A memo hit copies its tree, and Chakra's own-source style system built 39 GB of those copies in the first five components without many requests, so reading only between components or requests is too late. The budget is 60% of the memory the process may use, at most 8 GiB (`HeapBudget::machine`): the physical memory, or on Linux the lowest memory limit of its cgroup and their ancestors (`/proc/self/cgroup`, v2 `memory.max`, v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes`) when lower, so a container or CI job with a limit gets a budget under it; there is no option for it. Past it the run takes no further step: the conversion in flight stops, every component not yet answered keeps its structural result, and one `SEMANTIC_BACKEND` warning names them and the heap it read. **Past the budget the output depends on timing** (how far each lane had got), as the warning says, and such an answer is not kept in the cache. Under it nothing changes. Measured peak commits with the budget at 8 GiB: Mantine core 1.1 GiB, shadcn 1.1 GiB, ant-design 0.96 GiB, react-spectrum 1.0 GiB, `gate-large` 1.1 GiB, `chakra-only` 0.96 GiB; Chakra's `packages/react/src` stops at 8.1 GiB (4.7 GiB with a 4 GiB budget) where it reached 42 GB. The arena bound above and the `OnDemand` session are unchanged: they do not run under the budget.
- **Converted on the checker's thread:** an answer is converted on the checker's own thread (`Client::run_on_thread`), in a runtime of its own there, so each of its requests (about 3,200 for Chakra's `Button`) is answered in place instead of crossing a channel to the checker and back. The guards are the same: a panic in the session ends it, each request is bounded by `request_timeout` (past it the answer stops waiting and the work's later requests fail, a release excepted), and a panic in the conversion itself leaves the session answering. The first answer for `ChakraButton` went from 145 to 115 ms, and one edit-and-query of `ButtonProps` (`watch`) from 152 to 119 ms at the median (load 6 to 9; these include the reference and prop-key allocation changes).
- **Start and stop:** creating the checker and `warm_up` return at once, and dropping the checker waits at most `shutdown_wait` (5 s) for a request in progress before letting the worker finish alone. The checker's thread finishes a request in progress, then closes its session and exits.
- **Warm-up snapshot:** `warm_up` also builds the snapshot the first request starts from: a program rooted at a file held in the checker's memory (never on disk) that imports each package the nearest `package.json` lists under `dependencies` and `peerDependencies` (`@types` packages are read anyway). Its files are stamped like a request's. The first request brings it up to date with `updateSnapshot`, re-rooted at its own files and with announced edits read again, instead of reading the lib and every dependency from the disk with `createSnapshot`; the warm snapshot is then released. An edit nobody announced is caught as for any kept snapshot. The memory bound is checked after the warm-up too. On `gate-large` (Chakra and MUI) the warm-up takes 63 to 77 ms, its arenas hold 38 MiB, and after the first answer they hold 49 to 50 MiB instead of 40 (peak RSS 20 to 35 MiB higher); `ChakraButton`'s first answer went from 146 to 156 ms to 126 to 149 ms (load 7 to 9).
- **Tests:** `crates/semantic/tests/on_demand.rs` asks the built-in checker.
- **Latency, re-measured** (`ondemand_bench`, 30 components, release build, `7.1.0-beta`): shadcn first answer 84 ms, median 21 ms, p90 37 ms; antd first 93 ms, median 36 ms, p90 40 ms. The memory check does not add to a story's wait.

## The algorithm

Mirrors RDT 2.4.0 (`lib/parser.js`). Method names are from the 7.1 client.

1. `getSymbolOfSourceFile(file)`, then `getExportsOfModule`.
2. For each export, `getTypeOfSymbol`, then `getSignaturesOfType(Call)`. A component has a signature whose first parameter is named `props` or is the only parameter. For a class, use `Construct` signatures and read `props` from the instance type.
3. Props type: `getTypeOfSymbolAtLocation(param, param.valueDeclaration)`. Props: the type's apparent properties, plus each member's when it is a union.
4. Per prop, `type` is `typeToString(getBaseConstraintOfType(t) ?? t)` with default flags, so long types truncate as they do in RDT. `required` means the symbol lacks `Optional` and has no code default.
5. `parent` is the first declaration's parent when that is an interface or type alias. `declarations` is every declaration's parent.
6. `description` and `tags` come from `getDocumentationComment` and `getJsDocTags`.

RDT also emits any exported symbol that has a JSDoc comment but no props. We don't. In the fixture corpus, 23 of the 26 entries only RDT emits are of this kind, such as enum members, type aliases and functions.

### The converter (ADR 0026, slice S2)

A prop's checker type becomes a `PropType` from structured answers only (`crates/semantic/src/convert.rs`): the type flags, a union's members (`getTypesOfType`), a reference's arguments, a tuple type's element flags (`getTargetOfType`), an object's signatures, properties and index signatures (one `batchRequests`), and an alias's symbol and arguments. `typeToString` is used for a name to display, and for two facts the API does not state: which parameter is optional and what a tuple element is labeled (`printed.rs` reads them from the printed type and refuses text that does not read to its end; a fact it cannot read is never replaced by a guess).

- **Named boundary.** An interface or class declared under `node_modules` or in the TypeScript lib (`Date`, `Promise<T>`, `HTMLElement`), and an object type a dependency's alias names, stay `named` with their arguments. A function type is always expanded. The lib's utilities (`Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `Record`) are expanded: their result is the type. A dependency's union of literals is expanded, since its members are the values a control offers. React's `ReactNode`, `ElementType`, `CSSProperties`, `ReactElement` and `JSX.Element` are recognized by where they are declared; `ReactElement` and `JSX.Element` stay `named` (`JSX.Element` named through its namespace, apart from the DOM's `Element`).
- **Caps.** Depth 5, 500 members at the top and 120 below it (a union, an intersection, a tuple's elements), and a budget of 100 properties at the top and 40 below it that counts only the members the project did not declare (inherited from a dependency or the lib, or with no declaration). A cut type is `truncated` with the limit (and, for a width, the total), which `degradedBy` reports. ## Boundaries

- **`crates/core`** owns the semantic result type, the merge and the diagnostics. It has no I/O, no async and no protocol types. The merge lives here because `OpaqueDetail` and `ParsedProp` internals are `pub(crate)`.
- **Backend crate** (`crates/semantic`, always compiled in and enabled at run time, ADR 0007) links the `tsrs` crates and asks them in process ("The checker"), runs the algorithm, and handles timeouts. Core never depends on it: the CLI runs the backend and calls core's `merge_semantic`.
- **CLI and NAPI** run it by default and turn it off on request. Neither calls JS.
- **Cold path only.** The hook is synchronous and runs on the cold path; `WatchSession::update_file` does not run it.
- **Failure** leaves the structural result and adds a diagnostic. It never fails extraction.
- **Determinism.** Reversing the query order changed no union order across 16 props in 3 files (2026-09-20). Whether canonical output sorts unions is open (below).

## The RDT oracle

`apps/oracle` depends on TypeScript 7.1 directly (for the oracle), but RDT 2.4.0 crashes on import against it (`ts.JsxEmit` is undefined). RDT now resolves its `typescript` peer to `typescript@6.0.3` instead, via the aliased `typescript-beta` dependency (`npm:typescript@7.1.0-beta`, pinned exactly) the oracle imports from — no pnpm override needed, since pnpm overrides don't reliably rewrite a peer dependency's resolution (tried `pnpm-workspace.yaml`'s `overrides: { "react-docgen-typescript>typescript": ... }`; the lockfile recorded it but RDT kept resolving against whatever `typescript` apps/oracle depended on directly).

The removed harness's `compare.ts`/`analyze.ts` (caliper-docgen vs RDT/react-docgen) compared only name, `required`, type and default, and rendered our types themselves in `run-ours.ts` (objects print as `{ ... }`), so their type mismatches mixed resolver and renderer differences. Those limits went with it: `scripts/weekly.py` compares Caliper's own and `@types/react` props with RDT's by name, and the oracle compares prop types structurally against the TS 7.1 checker (`docs/measurement.md`).

## Open decisions

1. **Output type.** Checker types don't fit `PropType` losslessly: `Named` has no file or symbol, and `Tuple` has no optional or rest elements (schema version 5 adds them, with labels and the other kinds ADR 0026's slice S1 lists). Add a variant or map into existing ones. `ExtractionOutput` carries `SCHEMA_VERSION`; a new variant bumps it.
2. **`ref` and `key`.** RDT emits both, and nothing else records forwardRef metadata. Semantic mode must match whatever the structural path does.
3. **Trigger.** Run on every exported component or only on files with degrade diagnostics. Bare generic parameters and TypeScript utility types resolve to `Named` with no diagnostic by design, so the second misses them.
4. **Union order.** Sort in canonical output, or keep source order for structural results.

# 0026. The checker is the type authority; oxc supplies syntax

**Status:** Accepted (2026-11-08) **Date:** 2026-11-07

## Context

ADR 0006 and 0007 made the TypeScript checker an opt-in second resolver, because a whole-project `tsc` run cost up to 9.3 s and 975 MiB (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`); ADR 0022 bounded it to a warm per-component request. The structural default still answers wrong without a marker: a type that is only a call signature becomes `{}`, `Omit`, `Pick` and `Partial` reached through an alias lose their effect, and a factory's props are taken from a name-matched interface (`docs/rdt-differences.md`, classes 4 to 6). A prototype found more: `[string, ...number[]]` prints as `[string, number[][]]` and a getter reads as a method. Each fix is another rule in a resolver that re-implements the type system.

tsrs (`oxc-project/tsrs`, Apache-2.0) is a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 checker at microsoft/TypeScript `3e9236361fa9`, the commit `typescript@7.1.0-beta` was built from. It speaks the same `--api` protocol: the 19 methods caliper calls are all present, and 87 one-prop fixtures got the same oracle verdicts as `typescript-beta`. A throwaway prototype through the Node client (not in the repository; these numbers are the record) measured on Chakra `ButtonProps` (1,138 props) a 43-47 ms snapshot and the first converted prop at 62-67 ms, where ADR 0022 measured 703 ms with `tsc` on a different program root (indicative, not an A/B), with tsrs peaking at 126-130 MiB. On 16 hand-written components the checker was equal or better on 14, worse on union member order and an unresolvable import. A polymorphic component instantiated through a virtual file gave 267 props for `'div'` where both engines give 2 today. tsrs's own benchmark (`bench/RESULTS.md`) reports 1.8 to 4.2 times TypeScript 7.1 beta's speed and 2.1 to 2.6 times less memory.

## Decision

The checker decides types and oxc decides syntax.

- **Authority.** The checker is the default source of a component's prop set, each prop's type, requiredness and description. oxc supplies candidate components (`extractor/evidence.rs`, `uses.rs`), defaults, JSDoc positions, source locations and declaration order, which is re-applied to union members because the checker sorts them by flags and value.
- **One projection model.** Checker facts convert once into the canonical model. Canonical JSON, TOON and the RDT view are projections of it, and no projection makes a type decision.
- **Fallback.** The structural resolver stays only for when the checker cannot answer: not installed or offline, an unsupported platform, a crash, a timeout. Its types carry `degradedBy` and the run carries one diagnostic.
- **Opt-out.** The checker runs unless `--no-checker` (`checker: false` in the config, the napi binding and the Storybook addon) turns it off; `--experimental-semantic-types` and `semanticTypes` are removed (S8).
- **Per surface.** The Storybook addon keeps ADR 0022: the structural answer first, the checker's within `semanticWaitMs`. Its premise that the checker is too slow for first paint was re-measured with tsrs in S4 and holds (Chakra's `Button`, 562 ms, 402 ms after the first-answer work). The CLI and agents wait for the checker, all candidates in one snapshot, with a timeout (10 s proposed).
- **Pin.** We pin exact tsrs crates (`tsrs_api` and `tsrs_vfs` `=0.24.0`, TypeScript `3e9236361fa9`) and bump them on purpose, never through dependabot (its ignore list); the npm `tsrs` the parity gate runs (`apps/oracle`, `0.24.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, the same TypeScript commit) moves with them, and `scripts/check-packaging.mjs` fails while the two name different releases. A bump passes the deterministic construct suite (`apps/oracle/construct-suite`, being built on `feat/construct-suite`) and a tsrs-against-Go parity run of it. The weekly oracle keeps the Go `typescript` checker: an oracle running the checker that produced the answer agrees with it by construction.
- **Linked.** The product links the tsrs crates and asks `tsrs_api::Session` in process, on one thread with a 512 MiB stack, the stack the `tsrs` binary serves on; nothing is installed, and there is no other checker to choose. The Go `typescript` beta is the oracle, the construct goldens and the parity gate, in `apps/oracle` only. The linked checker is never replaced, since a fresh session raises this process's memory rather than returning it; past `OnDemandConfig::max_rss_mib`, read from its own arenas, it stops for the session and components keep their structural answer with a diagnostic. A panic closes its session and a fresh one answers the next request, and a file nested past 20,000 brackets is not given to it (trail 369 slice 2).
- **React element types.** The checker keeps `ReactElement` and `JSX.Element` as `named` types with their arguments, found by their declaration in `@types/react` (`JSX.Element` named through its namespace, apart from the DOM's `Element`); only `ReactNode` is the `reactNode` terminal. Amended 2026-11-13: this bullet first kept them collapsed to `reactNode`, which is wider (it also admits strings, numbers and `null`) and carried no `degradedBy`, so the construct suite's checker lane scored `react/03` to `05` less precise. The structural fallback still collapses them. No schema change: `named` already holds them.

Linked rather than spawned (trail 369): the crates are published (0.24.0), the same recorded Chakra answer (3,776 requests) takes 141 ms in process against 367 ms over the pipe with equal answers, and there is no per-platform binary to ship or find. What it costs: a stack overflow inside the checker aborts the host process (the 512 MiB thread holds a type 10,000 deep and tsrs's 256 MiB parse threads one 200,000 deep; past 20,000 brackets a file is refused, but nesting written without brackets, such as a chain of 700,000 arrow types, is not bounded), a dropped session does not return its memory (trail 369 slice 2, done: it bounds the checker's arenas and then answers structurally, [gate measurements](../gate-measurements.md#in-process-guards-trail-369-slice-2)), and each linked artifact grows by about 22 MB.

Trail 369 slice 4 (done, 2026-11-12) deleted the product's process route: `--tsc-path` and `tscPath` (CLI, config, napi, Storybook addon), `crates/tsc-client`, the binary lookup and the version allow-list it checked, and the replay tests that ran recordings of the Go checker through a fake `tsc` process; those tests ask the linked checker now. Slice 5's pin rule is in **Pin** above. Spawning a binary stays rejected (Alternatives).

## Consequences

- Supersedes "structural stays the default" in ADR 0006 and 0007 and 0007's "never a silent default" trigger. The rest of both stands.
- Deletable or shrinkable with a thin fallback, estimated from each file's header: in `crates/core/src/resolver`, `alias`, `chain`, `evaluate`, `substitute`, `named`, `primitives`, `extends`, `func`, `template`, `import`, `callee`, `memo`, `deps`, `collected` and `precedence` shrink to a no-generics subset and `mod.rs` by half; `dependency_types.rs` and `import_map.rs` go (the checker resolves modules; ADR 0010 and 0025 narrow to the fallback); in `extractor`, `interface` (but cva), `alias`, `values`, `reexports`, `asserted` and most of `visit` go, and `component`, `wrapper` and `mod.rs` shrink to candidate detection. About 7,600 of 25,300 non-test lines, 9,400 with no fallback, which Windows ARM64 rules out. `html`, `react`, `ambient`, `evidence`, `uses`, `defaults` and `jsdoc` stay; `crates/semantic` grows and `convert.rs` is rewritten (`crates/tsc-client`, the process route's client, is gone since trail 369 slice 4).
- Contract: `PropType` gains what the checker knows and it cannot hold: tuple element optional, rest and labels, `bigint`, `unique symbol`, enum identity, template literals, overload sets, call signatures on objects, a recursion marker, and a typed truncation in place of `Named` with checker text. React terminals (`ReactNode`, `CSSProperties`, `Ref`, `ElementType`, HTML attributes) are recognized by declaring path, as `is_react_declared` (`crates/semantic/src/component.rs`) does. `SCHEMA_VERSION` and `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (ADR 0017).
- No cache is keyed on a type id: ids are per checker and change with query order. Keys are file content, export name, instantiation and the tsrs pin. The checker does not see an edit it is not told about, so watch forwards every change. The whole-project `extract` keeps its answer on disk for the whole program only, keyed by every question its linked checker asked of the file system (failed lookups included) with a digest of each answer, the build's fingerprint (the pin with it) and the request; any different answer discards it whole (2026-11-12, `docs/type-checker-integration.md`).
- Unsolved: a per-component dependency closure from the checker (invalidation stays conservative), and the structural answer's gaps wherever the fallback runs.
- Risks: tsrs is pre-1.0, four releases in twelve days, and closed to pull requests (its README). Memory grew from 98 to 246 MB over 150 Chakra edits with each old snapshot disposed (#920 and #646 open). Determinism across checker counts is shown only on a 72-file program. There is no `@tsrs/win32-arm64` package, so those users get the fallback. The linked crates add about 22 MB to the CLI and to the napi binding.

## Alternatives considered

- **Keep the checker opt-in.** Two sources of truth, and the default keeps the silent wrong answers above.
- **Checker for the addon only.** The CLI and agents read the same wrong types, and they can afford to wait.
- **Spawn the `tsrs` binary** (`@tsrs/<platform>` with the npm packages). Process isolation and a restart lever, but the pipe costs more than the checker (367 against 141 ms on one answer), and every platform needs a binary found or shipped. Rejected; the route that ran one (`--tsc-path`) was deleted in trail 369 slice 4.
- **Parse with `tsrs_parser` instead of oxc.** Unpublished like every tsrs crate, and the extractor is written against oxc's AST, which already gives the syntactic facts kept here at about 2 ms per incremental update.
- **Keep investing in the structural resolver.** Each defect class above re-implements a checker rule and was silent until a comparison found it.
# Contributing

By participating in this project, you agree to abide by the [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Found a security issue? See [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue.

## Prerequisites

| Tool  | Min version   | Notes                                         |
| ----- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Rust  | 1.99          | `rustup update stable`                        |
| proto | latest        | manages Node/pnpm versions from `.prototools` |
| pnpm  | `.prototools` | via proto, or `npm i -g pnpm`                 |

After installing proto, run `moon setup` once to pull the pinned Node version and any other tool versions declared in `.prototools`.

## Build & test

```bash
# Rust
cargo build                                            # dev build
cargo test -p caliper-docgen-core                   # unit + snapshot tests
cargo clippy -p caliper-docgen-core -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all

# TypeScript
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test      # unit tests (mocked NAPI)
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test:integration  # integration tests (real native binding)

# Speed and memory of your branch against origin/main (Mantine and Chakra)
just bench
```

The pre-commit hook runs `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, `typos`, and `cargo deny` on every commit. It's fast enough that skipping it isn't worth the trouble.

## Snapshot tests

Snapshot tests use [insta](https://insta.rs). Each fixture (shadcn, MUI, Chakra, etc.) has a snapshot of the full extraction output. If your change touches extraction output, insta will flag it:

```bash
cargo test -p caliper-docgen-core    # fails with "snapshot mismatch"
cargo insta review                     # review diffs, accept or reject
```

Accept any snapshot change that is intentional (i.e., the output got more accurate). Reject regressions.

## Where code goes

**`crates/core`** — everything that understands TypeScript ASTs and React component patterns. No I/O, no async, no terminal output. Every function here must be `Send + Sync` so rayon can parallelize it.

**`crates/cli`** — user-facing output only. No extraction logic. Commands parse args and delegate to `core::pipeline`. Error formatting uses `miette`; progress uses `indicatif`; table output uses `comfy-table`.

**`crates/binding`** — thin NAPI wrapper. Owns the async runtime (tokio) and exposes the NAPI functions listed in `packages/napi/binding.d.ts` (batch extraction, sessions, and the lazy session's index, answers and warm-up). No business logic.

**`packages/napi`** — `caliper-docgen-napi`. TypeScript types (`index.d.ts`) and the dev binary loader (`index.js`) that finds the `.node` file from `target/` or `NAPI_RS_NATIVE_LIBRARY_PATH`. No logic.

**`packages/vite-plugin`** — `caliper-docgen-vite-plugin`. Single Vite `Plugin` object. No extraction logic — calls NAPI and manages HMR.

## Code style

The authoritative reference is `.claude/skills/rust-style/SKILL.md`. Highlights:

**Maps:** `FxHashMap` for internal maps (hot path, no DoS surface). `BTreeMap` for anything that ends up in JSON output (key ordering must be deterministic and stable across runs).

**Strings:** `CompactString` for type names and prop names. Most are ≤24 bytes (`string`, `boolean`, `ReactNode`, `MouseEvent`) and fit inline without heap allocation.

**Control flow:** `let...else` keeps the happy path flat:

```rust
let Some(entry) = map.get(key) else { return None };
```

**Matching on project-local enums:** no wildcards. `match status { Ok => .., Err => .. }` gives a compile error when new variants are added. `match status { Ok => .., _ => .. }` silently ignores them.

**No `unwrap()` outside tests.** Use `?` or emit a `Diagnostic` and return a safe default. The `Diagnostic` type has constructors for common error shapes.

**Comments:** only when the WHY is non-obvious. Not what the code does.

## Commits

- GPG-signed, `Signed-off-by` trailer (both configured in `.git/config`). `main` requires signed commits, so an unsigned commit in a pull request blocks the merge.
- `feat:` / `fix:` / `refactor:` / `chore:` / `docs:` prefix
- No line wrapping at any column
- Subject line says it all — skip the body if it adds nothing

```
# good
feat: resolve ComponentPropsWithoutRef in intersection type aliases

# bad
Updated the resolver to also handle the case where ComponentPropsWithoutRef
appears inside an intersection type alias, which was causing it to be
treated as opaque when it should expand the HTML attributes.
```

## Releases

Add a changeset for a consumer-visible change (`.changeset/`; see `AGENTS.md` for how to write one). Callisto (version pinned in `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`) plans the versions from the changesets and opens a release pull request (`callisto/version-packages`); merging it runs `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`, which publishes the crates and npm packages, tags each package, and publishes one GitHub Release for the CLI (`cargo/caliper-docgen@x.y.z`) with its changelog section as the notes and the five CLI binaries attached, each with a build attestation. The npm wrapper's tag `npm/caliper-docgen@x.y.z` is what the tap reads. `docs/releasing.md` has the release flow and how to recover a failed run.

Homebrew pulls from us: the tap's daily `brew bump` finds that tag with `livecheck`, builds `crates/cli` from source and bottles it, and a maintainer merges the formula pull request. Nothing in this repository notifies the tap.

Speed, memory and accuracy are recorded weekly and compared with the previous run (`docs/measurement.md`); there is no pull-request gate. Run `just bench` when a change touches the resolver.

## Pull requests

1. Branch from `main`
2. Keep the pre-commit hook passing
3. Update snapshots if extraction output changes (`cargo insta review`)
4. One logical change per PR — squash fixup commits before merging

> `just bench` is a local check of speed and memory against `main`; it prints a table and fails nothing. Accuracy against RDT and react-docgen is tracked by the weekly record (`docs/measurement.md`), not by a pull-request gate.

---
name: rust-style
description: Apply when writing or modifying Rust code in this project.
---

**Goal:** Code correct by construction, readable under churn, performant in hot paths.

## Project-specific decisions

These are non-negotiables, not preferences:

- Internal maps: `FxHashMap`. JSON-output maps: `BTreeMap` (deterministic key ordering).
- Type/prop names: `CompactString` — avoids heap allocation for strings ≤24 bytes.
- No `unwrap()` outside `#[cfg(test)]` — use `?` and let callers decide what to do with failure.

## Control flow

`let...else` keeps the happy path flat:

```rust
let Some(entry) = map.get(key) else { return None };
let Ok(parsed) = input.parse::<u32>() else { continue };
```

## Matching

No wildcards — a compile error on unhandled variants is a feature:

```rust
match status { Status::Ok => .., Status::Err => .. }  // compiler tells you when Status grows
match status { Status::Ok => .., _ => .. }             // silently misses new variants
```

Full `match` over `matches!` for the same reason.

## Types

Newtypes when a bare type allows confusion. Enums when a bool parameter hides intent:

```rust
struct ScopedKey(CompactString);         // not: String
enum Visibility { Public, Private }      // not: is_public: bool
```

Explicit destructuring gets compiler errors when structs change:

```rust
let ComponentEntry { display_name, file_path, .. } = entry;
```

## Naming

Shadow variables through transformations — no `raw_`/`parsed_`/`trimmed_` prefixes:

```rust
let path = args.path;
let path = path.canonicalize()?;
let path = path.join("config.toml");
```

## Comments

Only when the WHY is non-obvious: a hidden constraint, a workaround, a non-obvious invariant. Not what the code does.

# Contributing

By participating in this project, you agree to abide by the [Code of Conduct](./CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). Found a security issue? See [SECURITY.md](./SECURITY.md) instead of opening a public issue.

## Prerequisites

| Tool  | Min version   | Notes                                         |
| ----- | ------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Rust  | 1.99          | `rustup update stable`                        |
| proto | latest        | manages Node/pnpm versions from `.prototools` |
| pnpm  | `.prototools` | via proto, or `npm i -g pnpm`                 |

After installing proto, run `moon setup` once to pull the pinned Node version and any other tool versions declared in `.prototools`.

## Build & test

```bash
# Rust
cargo build                                            # dev build
cargo test -p caliper-docgen-core                   # unit + snapshot tests
cargo clippy -p caliper-docgen-core -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all

# TypeScript
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test      # unit tests (mocked NAPI)
pnpm --filter caliper-docgen-vite-plugin test:integration  # integration tests (real native binding)

# Speed and memory of your branch against origin/main (Mantine and Chakra)
just bench
```

The pre-commit hook runs `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings`, `typos`, and `cargo deny` on every commit. It's fast enough that skipping it isn't worth the trouble.

## Snapshot tests

Snapshot tests use [insta](https://insta.rs). Each fixture (shadcn, MUI, Chakra, etc.) has a snapshot of the full extraction output. If your change touches extraction output, insta will flag it:

```bash
cargo test -p caliper-docgen-core    # fails with "snapshot mismatch"
cargo insta review                     # review diffs, accept or reject
```

Accept any snapshot change that is intentional (i.e., the output got more accurate). Reject regressions.

## Where code goes

**`crates/core`** — everything that understands TypeScript ASTs and React component patterns. No I/O, no async, no terminal output. Every function here must be `Send + Sync` so rayon can parallelize it.

**`crates/cli`** — user-facing output only. No extraction logic. Commands parse args and delegate to `core::pipeline`. Error formatting uses `miette`; progress uses `indicatif`; table output uses `comfy-table`.

**`crates/binding`** — thin NAPI wrapper. Owns the async runtime (tokio) and exposes the NAPI functions listed in `packages/napi/binding.d.ts` (batch extraction, sessions, and the lazy session's index, answers and warm-up). No business logic.

**`packages/napi`** — `caliper-docgen-napi`. TypeScript types (`index.d.ts`) and the dev binary loader (`index.js`) that finds the `.node` file from `target/` or `NAPI_RS_NATIVE_LIBRARY_PATH`. No logic.

**`packages/vite-plugin`** — `caliper-docgen-vite-plugin`. Single Vite `Plugin` object. No extraction logic — calls NAPI and manages HMR.

## Code style

The authoritative reference is `.claude/skills/rust-style/SKILL.md`. Highlights:

**Maps:** `FxHashMap` for internal maps (hot path, no DoS surface). `BTreeMap` for anything that ends up in JSON output (key ordering must be deterministic and stable across runs).

**Strings:** `CompactString` for type names and prop names. Most are ≤24 bytes (`string`, `boolean`, `ReactNode`, `MouseEvent`) and fit inline without heap allocation.

**Control flow:** `let...else` keeps the happy path flat:

```rust
let Some(entry) = map.get(key) else { return None };
```

**Matching on project-local enums:** no wildcards. `match status { Ok => .., Err => .. }` gives a compile error when new variants are added. `match status { Ok => .., _ => .. }` silently ignores them.

**No `unwrap()` outside tests.** Use `?` or emit a `Diagnostic` and return a safe default. The `Diagnostic` type has constructors for common error shapes.

**Comments:** only when the WHY is non-obvious. Not what the code does.

## Commits

- GPG-signed, `Signed-off-by` trailer (both configured in `.git/config`). `main` requires signed commits, so an unsigned commit in a pull request blocks the merge.
- `feat:` / `fix:` / `refactor:` / `chore:` / `docs:` prefix
- No line wrapping at any column
- Subject line says it all — skip the body if it adds nothing

```
# good
feat: resolve ComponentPropsWithoutRef in intersection type aliases

# bad
Updated the resolver to also handle the case where ComponentPropsWithoutRef
appears inside an intersection type alias, which was causing it to be
treated as opaque when it should expand the HTML attributes.
```

## Releases

Add a changeset for a consumer-visible change (`.changeset/`; see `AGENTS.md` for how to write one). Callisto (version pinned in `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`) plans the versions from the changesets and opens a release pull request (`callisto/version-packages`); merging it runs `.github/workflows/callisto-release.yml`, which publishes the crates and npm packages, tags each package, and publishes one GitHub Release for the CLI (`cargo/caliper-docgen@x.y.z`) with its changelog section as the notes and the five CLI binaries attached, each with a build attestation. The npm wrapper's tag `npm/caliper-docgen@x.y.z` is what the tap reads. `docs/releasing.md` has the release flow and how to recover a failed run.

Homebrew pulls from us: the tap's daily `brew bump` finds that tag with `livecheck`, builds `crates/cli` from source and bottles it, and a maintainer merges the formula pull request. Nothing in this repository notifies the tap.

Speed, memory and accuracy are recorded weekly and compared with the previous run (`docs/measurement.md`); there is no pull-request gate. Run `just bench` when a change touches the resolver.

## Pull requests

1. Branch from `main`
2. Keep the pre-commit hook passing
3. Update snapshots if extraction output changes (`cargo insta review`)
4. One logical change per PR — squash fixup commits before merging

> `just bench` is a local check of speed and memory against `main`; it prints a table and fails nothing. Accuracy against RDT and react-docgen is tracked by the weekly record (`docs/measurement.md`), not by a pull-request gate.

# 0026. The checker is the type authority; oxc supplies syntax

**Status:** Accepted (2026-11-08) **Date:** 2026-11-07

## Context

ADR 0006 and 0007 made the TypeScript checker an opt-in second resolver, because a whole-project `tsc` run cost up to 9.3 s and 975 MiB (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`); ADR 0022 bounded it to a warm per-component request. The structural default still answers wrong without a marker: a type that is only a call signature becomes `{}`, `Omit`, `Pick` and `Partial` reached through an alias lose their effect, and a factory's props are taken from a name-matched interface (`docs/rdt-differences.md`, classes 4 to 6). A prototype found more: `[string, ...number[]]` prints as `[string, number[][]]` and a getter reads as a method. Each fix is another rule in a resolver that re-implements the type system.

tsrs (`oxc-project/tsrs`, Apache-2.0) is a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 checker at microsoft/TypeScript `3e9236361fa9`, the commit `typescript@7.1.0-beta` was built from. It speaks the same `--api` protocol: the 19 methods caliper calls are all present, and 87 one-prop fixtures got the same oracle verdicts as `typescript-beta`. A throwaway prototype through the Node client (not in the repository; these numbers are the record) measured on Chakra `ButtonProps` (1,138 props) a 43-47 ms snapshot and the first converted prop at 62-67 ms, where ADR 0022 measured 703 ms with `tsc` on a different program root (indicative, not an A/B), with tsrs peaking at 126-130 MiB. On 16 hand-written components the checker was equal or better on 14, worse on union member order and an unresolvable import. A polymorphic component instantiated through a virtual file gave 267 props for `'div'` where both engines give 2 today. tsrs's own benchmark (`bench/RESULTS.md`) reports 1.8 to 4.2 times TypeScript 7.1 beta's speed and 2.1 to 2.6 times less memory.

## Decision

The checker decides types and oxc decides syntax.

- **Authority.** The checker is the default source of a component's prop set, each prop's type, requiredness and description. oxc supplies candidate components (`extractor/evidence.rs`, `uses.rs`), defaults, JSDoc positions, source locations and declaration order, which is re-applied to union members because the checker sorts them by flags and value.
- **One projection model.** Checker facts convert once into the canonical model. Canonical JSON, TOON and the RDT view are projections of it, and no projection makes a type decision.
- **Fallback.** The structural resolver stays only for when the checker cannot answer: not installed or offline, an unsupported platform, a crash, a timeout. Its types carry `degradedBy` and the run carries one diagnostic.
- **Opt-out.** The checker runs unless `--no-checker` (`checker: false` in the config, the napi binding and the Storybook addon) turns it off; `--experimental-semantic-types` and `semanticTypes` are removed (S8).
- **Per surface.** The Storybook addon keeps ADR 0022: the structural answer first, the checker's within `semanticWaitMs`. Its premise that the checker is too slow for first paint was re-measured with tsrs in S4 and holds (Chakra's `Button`, 562 ms, 402 ms after the first-answer work). The CLI and agents wait for the checker, all candidates in one snapshot, with a timeout (10 s proposed).
- **Pin.** We pin exact tsrs crates (`tsrs_api` and `tsrs_vfs` `=0.24.0`, TypeScript `3e9236361fa9`) and bump them on purpose, never through dependabot (its ignore list); the npm `tsrs` the parity gate runs (`apps/oracle`, `0.24.0-ts7.1.0-beta`, the same TypeScript commit) moves with them, and `scripts/check-packaging.mjs` fails while the two name different releases. A bump passes the deterministic construct suite (`apps/oracle/construct-suite`, being built on `feat/construct-suite`) and a tsrs-against-Go parity run of it. The weekly oracle keeps the Go `typescript` checker: an oracle running the checker that produced the answer agrees with it by construction.
- **Linked.** The product links the tsrs crates and asks `tsrs_api::Session` in process, on one thread with a 512 MiB stack, the stack the `tsrs` binary serves on; nothing is installed, and there is no other checker to choose. The Go `typescript` beta is the oracle, the construct goldens and the parity gate, in `apps/oracle` only. The linked checker is never replaced, since a fresh session raises this process's memory rather than returning it; past `OnDemandConfig::max_rss_mib`, read from its own arenas, it stops for the session and components keep their structural answer with a diagnostic. A panic closes its session and a fresh one answers the next request, and a file nested past 20,000 brackets is not given to it (trail 369 slice 2).
- **React element types.** The checker keeps `ReactElement` and `JSX.Element` as `named` types with their arguments, found by their declaration in `@types/react` (`JSX.Element` named through its namespace, apart from the DOM's `Element`); only `ReactNode` is the `reactNode` terminal. Amended 2026-11-13: this bullet first kept them collapsed to `reactNode`, which is wider (it also admits strings, numbers and `null`) and carried no `degradedBy`, so the construct suite's checker lane scored `react/03` to `05` less precise. The structural fallback still collapses them. No schema change: `named` already holds them.

Linked rather than spawned (trail 369): the crates are published (0.24.0), the same recorded Chakra answer (3,776 requests) takes 141 ms in process against 367 ms over the pipe with equal answers, and there is no per-platform binary to ship or find. What it costs: a stack overflow inside the checker aborts the host process (the 512 MiB thread holds a type 10,000 deep and tsrs's 256 MiB parse threads one 200,000 deep; past 20,000 brackets a file is refused, but nesting written without brackets, such as a chain of 700,000 arrow types, is not bounded), a dropped session does not return its memory (trail 369 slice 2, done: it bounds the checker's arenas and then answers structurally, [gate measurements](../gate-measurements.md#in-process-guards-trail-369-slice-2)), and each linked artifact grows by about 22 MB.

Trail 369 slice 4 (done, 2026-11-12) deleted the product's process route: `--tsc-path` and `tscPath` (CLI, config, napi, Storybook addon), `crates/tsc-client`, the binary lookup and the version allow-list it checked, and the replay tests that ran recordings of the Go checker through a fake `tsc` process; those tests ask the linked checker now. Slice 5's pin rule is in **Pin** above. Spawning a binary stays rejected (Alternatives).

## Consequences

- Supersedes "structural stays the default" in ADR 0006 and 0007 and 0007's "never a silent default" trigger. The rest of both stands.
- Deletable or shrinkable with a thin fallback, estimated from each file's header: in `crates/core/src/resolver`, `alias`, `chain`, `evaluate`, `substitute`, `named`, `primitives`, `extends`, `func`, `template`, `import`, `callee`, `memo`, `deps`, `collected` and `precedence` shrink to a no-generics subset and `mod.rs` by half; `dependency_types.rs` and `import_map.rs` go (the checker resolves modules; ADR 0010 and 0025 narrow to the fallback); in `extractor`, `interface` (but cva), `alias`, `values`, `reexports`, `asserted` and most of `visit` go, and `component`, `wrapper` and `mod.rs` shrink to candidate detection. About 7,600 of 25,300 non-test lines, 9,400 with no fallback, which Windows ARM64 rules out. `html`, `react`, `ambient`, `evidence`, `uses`, `defaults` and `jsdoc` stay; `crates/semantic` grows and `convert.rs` is rewritten (`crates/tsc-client`, the process route's client, is gone since trail 369 slice 4).
- Contract: `PropType` gains what the checker knows and it cannot hold: tuple element optional, rest and labels, `bigint`, `unique symbol`, enum identity, template literals, overload sets, call signatures on objects, a recursion marker, and a typed truncation in place of `Named` with checker text. React terminals (`ReactNode`, `CSSProperties`, `Ref`, `ElementType`, HTML attributes) are recognized by declaring path, as `is_react_declared` (`crates/semantic/src/component.rs`) does. `SCHEMA_VERSION` and `CACHE_SCHEMA_VERSION` bump (ADR 0017).
- No cache is keyed on a type id: ids are per checker and change with query order. Keys are file content, export name, instantiation and the tsrs pin. The checker does not see an edit it is not told about, so watch forwards every change. The whole-project `extract` keeps its answer on disk for the whole program only, keyed by every question its linked checker asked of the file system (failed lookups included) with a digest of each answer, the build's fingerprint (the pin with it) and the request; any different answer discards it whole (2026-11-12, `docs/type-checker-integration.md`).
- Unsolved: a per-component dependency closure from the checker (invalidation stays conservative), and the structural answer's gaps wherever the fallback runs.
- Risks: tsrs is pre-1.0, four releases in twelve days, and closed to pull requests (its README). Memory grew from 98 to 246 MB over 150 Chakra edits with each old snapshot disposed (#920 and #646 open). Determinism across checker counts is shown only on a 72-file program. There is no `@tsrs/win32-arm64` package, so those users get the fallback. The linked crates add about 22 MB to the CLI and to the napi binding.

Migration, each slice behind a deterministic gate, none on the oracle. The tsrs backend (the Rust client running on tsrs, PR 390) is done.

1. **S1** (done) Shared projection model and the new `PropType` variants, filled by the structural path where it knows them. Gate: a unit test per variant, golden JSON diff, cache schema test.
2. **S2** (done) Flag-based converter in `convert.rs`, memoized by type id within one snapshot, with a named-boundary policy and caps. Gate: the construct suite's expected JSON; reversed query order gives identical bytes.
3. **S3** (done) React terminals by declaring path. Gate: no regression against today's Chakra `Button` terminals.
4. **S4** (done, one gate failed) The checker's answer wins when it runs: the addon inside ADR 0022's window, the CLI waiting (`--semantic-timeout-ms`, 10 s), and a prop the checker could not read keeps its structural type with `degradedBy` (`docs/type-checker-integration.md`). Gate: checker-on output equals structural on the suite except a listed set of improvements (held by the checker lane); Chakra first answer at most 150 ms through the Rust client (measured 562 ms, then 402 ms once each answer was parsed once and a type's parts asked for once; FAIL: the floor of that request set with no round trips is about 230 ms, 81% of its bytes the property lists of Chakra's style-prop condition maps, so the seam has to change rather than the budget: [gate measurements](../gate-measurements.md#first-answer-s4), and ADR 0022's structural-first answer stands); the Storybook harness re-run (not run: it needs the corpora).
5. **S5** (done) Instantiation of generic and polymorphic components through a virtual file: a component whose first type parameter declares a default is read at it, from a file the checker holds in memory (`createSnapshot`'s `fileSystem` layer, read by tsrs and the Go beta alike) in a second snapshot made only when a requested component is generic; an instantiation that does not form keeps the structural props with the checker's error as the reason ([generic components](../type-checker-integration.md#generic-components-adr-0026-slice-s5)). Gate: `Poly<'div'>` gives at least 260 props and `'a'` differs (PASS: 281 and 289, on tsrs and the Go checker, `crates/semantic/tests/instantiate.rs`).
6. **S6** (done, one gate failed) Watch on `snapshot.update` with RSS recycling: the warm checker keeps its snapshot and brings it up to date with `updateSnapshot` (`ensurePrograms`, the files the session announced), and before an answer compares every file its program read with the stamp it had; an unannounced change answers from a fresh snapshot with a warning naming the file ([watch](../type-checker-integration.md#watch-adr-0026-slice-s6)). Gate: an unnotified edit fails a test loudly (PASS, `crates/semantic/tests/watch.rs`, on tsrs and the Go checker); Chakra edit-and-query p95 at most 25 ms (PASS at 22.6 ms for a component with props of its own in the Chakra program; FAIL at 565 ms and more for one of Chakra's `ButtonProps`, whose floor is converting its 1,140 props, 330 ms on an unchanged snapshot, while the checker's CPU per edit fell from 437 to 737 ms to 56 to 70: [gate measurements](../gate-measurements.md#watch-on-snapshotupdate-s6)); 300 Chakra edits stay under the threshold (PASS, peak 321 to 357 MiB against 768, 5 `worn` replacements, answers byte-identical to a fresh session's).
7. **S7** Delete the structural resolver for what the suite covers. Gate: every suite row passes with the fallback off on supported platforms; a Windows ARM64 job runs the fallback. (Windows was dropped as a supported platform afterwards, trail 370, so that job no longer exists.)
